graph.name: Epistemological Worldview Network
graph.description: A philosophical state-transition and pressure network modeling how metaphysical, historical, moral, existential, social, and experiential evidence can move an agent among naturalism, agnosticism, theism, religious traditions, secular humanism, and historic Christianity. The graph intentionally supports cycles and competing attractors.

weight_semantics.description: Positive weights indicate evidential/supportive pressure toward the target node; negative weights indicate defeater/counter-pressure. Magnitude represents rough relative influence, not empirical probability.

graph.stage_semantics: Typical epistemic availability/depth, not mandatory chronology.

nodes.label: Human person inside reality
nodes.description: The epistemic agent whose worldview is being updated by argument, evidence, experience, history, and social context.

nodes.label: What is ultimately real?
nodes.description: Metaphysical inquiry into the nature and ground of reality.

nodes.label: What can I know?
nodes.description: Epistemological inquiry into warrant, rationality, evidence, and certainty.

nodes.label: What happened?
nodes.description: Historical inquiry into publicly accessible claims and events.

nodes.label: What is ultimately good?
nodes.description: Moral and existential inquiry into value, purpose, flourishing, and obligation.

nodes.label: Love and attachment
nodes.description: Experience of self-giving love, relational value, and attachment to persons.

nodes.label: Beauty and awe
nodes.description: Aesthetic experience of beauty, sublimity, harmony, and transcendence.

nodes.label: Moral obligation and guilt
nodes.description: Experience that some actions are genuinely right, wrong, owed, or forbidden.

nodes.label: Suffering and death
nodes.description: Encounter with pain, mortality, tragedy, cruelty, loss, and apparent futility.

nodes.label: Consciousness and first-person awareness
nodes.description: Immediate experience of subjectivity, intentionality, reason, and selfhood.

nodes.label: Longing and transcendence
nodes.description: Persistent desire for meaning, permanence, communion, or fulfillment beyond finite goods.

nodes.label: Forgiveness and reconciliation
nodes.description: Experience that genuine reconciliation can acknowledge debt while absorbing its cost.

nodes.label: Religious / mystical experience
nodes.description: Experiences interpreted as divine presence, transcendence, encounter, or sacredness.

nodes.label: Contingency / sufficient reason
nodes.description: Why contingent reality exists rather than nothing.

nodes.label: Kalam cosmological argument
nodes.description: Pressure from a finite or caused cosmos toward a transcendent cause.

nodes.label: Transcendental argument
nodes.description: Pressure from logic, rational normativity, intelligibility, or preconditions of knowledge.

nodes.label: Intelligibility of the universe
nodes.description: The apparent fit among mathematics, rational minds, and physical law.

nodes.label: Argument from consciousness
nodes.description: Pressure from first-person subjectivity against exhaustive reductive physicalism.

nodes.label: Moral argument
nodes.description: Pressure from objective moral facts, duties, and intrinsic human value.

nodes.label: Argument from personhood
nodes.description: Pressure from the apparent intrinsic value and irreducibility of persons.

nodes.label: Aesthetic argument
nodes.description: Weak-to-moderate pressure from beauty as potentially objective or revelatory.

nodes.label: Argument from desire / longing
nodes.description: Abductive pressure from persistent transcendent longing; not deductive proof.

nodes.label: Scientific explanatory success
nodes.description: Natural explanations successfully account for large domains of observed reality.

nodes.label: Evolutionary explanation
nodes.description: Biological complexity and behavior arise through natural processes without continual intervention.

nodes.label: Brain-mind dependence
nodes.description: Strong correlation of mental life with physical brain states supports physicalist interpretations.

nodes.label: Logical problem of evil
nodes.description: Evil is argued to be logically incompatible with a God who is all-powerful, all-knowing and wholly good.

nodes.label: Problem of animal suffering
nodes.description: Pre-human predation, disease, pain, and extinction challenge many free-will or soul-making defenses.

nodes.label: Divine hiddenness
nodes.description: Sincere nonbelief and ambiguous divine presence pressure against a perfectly loving personal God.

nodes.label: Religious diversity
nodes.description: Conflicting sincere religious claims reduce confidence in any single revelatory tradition.

nodes.label: Low prior probability of miracles
nodes.description: Under naturalism, resurrection and miracle claims begin with severe prior improbability.

nodes.label: Textual and doctrinal tensions
nodes.description: Internal interpretive disputes, difficult texts, and doctrinal complexity create epistemic friction.

nodes.label: Church scandal and hypocrisy
nodes.description: Moral failure of religious institutions can operate as evidential and emotional counter-pressure.

nodes.label: Religious trauma / bad witness
nodes.description: Harm associated with religious communities can close or distort further inquiry.

nodes.label: Moral conflict with doctrine
nodes.description: Perceived incompatibility between doctrine and moral intuitions can drive deconstruction.

nodes.label: Institutional distrust
nodes.description: Suspicion that institutions preserve power or tradition rather than truth.

nodes.label: Argument fatigue / epistemic closure
nodes.description: Repeated unresolved dispute may lead an agent to stop engaging competing arguments.

nodes.label: Radical uncertainty
nodes.description: No worldview has yet gained decisive explanatory priority.

nodes.label: Naturalism highly competitive
nodes.description: Naturalism offers strong explanatory simplicity and empirical continuity.

nodes.label: Transcendence plausible
nodes.description: A ground beyond contingent physical reality becomes plausible.

nodes.label: Mind-like ground plausible
nodes.description: Ultimate reality appears increasingly compatible with reason, mind, normativity, or personhood.

nodes.label: Personal theism
nodes.description: A personal, rational, transcendent divine ground becomes the leading metaphysical hypothesis.

nodes.label: Impersonal / transpersonal absolute
nodes.description: Ultimate reality is conceived as impersonal, nondual, structural, or transpersonal.

nodes.label: Tentative theism
nodes.description: Theism remains plausible but evil, hiddenness, and uncertainty prevent confident commitment.

nodes.label: Agnostic naturalism
nodes.description: Naturalism is favored while metaphysical uncertainty remains.

nodes.label: Secular humanism
nodes.description: Human dignity, ethics, and meaning are retained without transcendent revelation.

nodes.label: Epistemically closed posture
nodes.description: The agent ceases meaningful engagement with counterarguments or alternative hypotheses.

nodes.label: Christianity leading hypothesis
nodes.description: Christianity becomes the strongest current explanatory model, though not yet full commitment.

nodes.label: Historic / apostolic Christianity
nodes.description: Christian commitment interpreted through historic ecclesial, sacramental, and creedal categories.

nodes.label: Christian commitment with unresolved tensions
nodes.description: Christianity is affirmed while evil, hiddenness, pluralism, and interpretive problems remain real.

nodes.label: Judaism
nodes.description: The historical covenantal and monotheistic matrix from which Christianity emerges.

nodes.label: Christianity
nodes.description: Claims that God uniquely acts and reveals himself in Jesus Christ.

nodes.label: Islam
nodes.description: Strict monotheism, prophetic revelation, Qur'an, and later reinterpretation of Jesus.

nodes.label: Hindu traditions
nodes.description: Plural family of metaphysical, devotional, ritual, and liberation traditions.

nodes.label: Buddhist traditions
nodes.description: Non-theistic or differently-theistic traditions centered on suffering, impermanence, and liberation.

nodes.label: Revelation becomes a live possibility
nodes.description: If personal theism is plausible, alleged divine self-disclosure becomes evidence worth testing.

nodes.label: Comparative religious investigation
nodes.description: Religious traditions are compared historically, philosophically, morally, and phenomenologically.

nodes.label: Jesus of Nazareth
nodes.description: The first-century Jewish teacher around whom Christianity emerges.

nodes.label: Crucifixion of Jesus
nodes.description: Jesus is executed under Roman authority; a high-confidence historical datum.

nodes.label: Empty tomb tradition
nodes.description: Early Christian claim that Jesus' burial place was found empty.

nodes.label: Post-death appearance traditions
nodes.description: Claims that individuals and groups experienced Jesus alive after his death.

nodes.label: Transformation of disciples
nodes.description: Followers move from defeat to public resurrection proclamation.

nodes.label: Paul and James
nodes.description: Early conversions/transformations treated as data requiring explanation.

nodes.label: Early exalted devotion to Jesus
nodes.description: Very early Jewish-Christian devotion assigns Jesus extraordinary divine significance.

nodes.label: What best explains the resurrection data?
nodes.description: The central historical bottleneck in the Christian hypothesis space.

nodes.label: Naturalistic resurrection explanations
nodes.description: Vision, legend, cognitive dissonance, memory development, social dynamics, or mixed natural mechanisms.

nodes.label: Actual bodily resurrection
nodes.description: God raised Jesus from the dead.

nodes.label: Jesus' epistemic authority upgraded
nodes.description: If resurrection is likely, Jesus' teachings gain substantially greater evidential weight.

nodes.label: Christology
nodes.description: Inquiry into Jesus' divine/human identity.

nodes.label: Incarnation
nodes.description: The transcendent Creator genuinely enters embodied human history.

nodes.label: Cross as self-giving reconciliation
nodes.description: Evil is neither ignored nor ultimate; reconciliation occurs through costly self-giving.

nodes.label: Trinitarian ontology
nodes.description: Ultimate reality is one divine being whose life eternally contains relation and love.

nodes.label: Scripture reread through Christ
nodes.description: Biblical texts are recursively reinterpreted in light of resurrection and Christology.

nodes.label: Resurrection and cosmic restoration
nodes.description: Creation, embodiment, and persons are restored rather than discarded.

nodes.label: Church / sacrament / apostolic community
nodes.description: Conversion leads into visible communal, sacramental, and apostolic questions.

nodes.label: Early post-apostolic Christianity
nodes.description: Ignatius, Clement, Justin, Irenaeus and others provide evidence about early ecclesial Christianity.

nodes.label: Objective value / moral realism
nodes.description: Moral claims are treated as more than individual or social preference.

nodes.label: Intrinsic dignity of persons
nodes.description: Persons are experienced as ends possessing value that exceeds instrumental utility.

nodes.label: Value may be fundamental
nodes.description: Goodness, beauty, or normativity may belong to reality rather than being wholly projected.

nodes.label: Meaning constructed rather than discovered
nodes.description: Meaning is humanly generated within an indifferent or non-teleological cosmos.

nodes.label: Naturalistic moral realism / anti-realism
nodes.description: Secular accounts ground, reconstruct, or deflate morality without divine command.

nodes.label: Attractor: Resurrection
nodes.description: High-centrality historical attractor. If rejected, historic Christianity collapses; if accepted, it recursively updates earlier metaphysical priors.

nodes.label: Attractor: Love
nodes.description: Existential attractor connecting personhood, morality, forgiveness, Trinity, cross, and ultimate value.

nodes.label: Attractor: Naturalistic simplicity
nodes.description: Explanatory attractor favoring a worldview in which suffering, hiddenness, and causal closure require no divine reason.

nodes.label: Attractor: Global explanatory coherence
nodes.description: Meta-attractor favoring the worldview that best integrates metaphysics, history, morality, experience, and explanatory cost.

nodes.label: Residual tension: evil and suffering
nodes.description: Christianity must reconcile divine goodness with apparently gratuitous suffering.

nodes.label: Residual tension: divine hiddenness
nodes.description: Christianity must explain sincere nonbelief and ambiguous divine presence.

nodes.label: Residual tension: religious pluralism
nodes.description: Christianity must account for sincere competing revelations and traditions.

nodes.label: Residual tension: church failure
nodes.description: The moral witness of Christianity is compromised by institutional and personal failures.

nodes.label: Residual tension: consciousness
nodes.description: Naturalism must explain subjectivity and intentional awareness.

nodes.label: Residual tension: normativity
nodes.description: Naturalism must account for logical, moral, and rational oughts.

nodes.label: Residual tension: intrinsic value
nodes.description: Naturalism must explain whether persons and values are objectively significant.

nodes.label: Residual tension: existence and intelligibility
nodes.description: Naturalism may leave the existence and rational structure of reality as brute facts.

nodes.label: Atheism
nodes.description: The positive judgment that no God exists, as distinct from suspending judgment.

nodes.label: Classical theism
nodes.description: God as the simple, necessary ground of being, reached mainly through metaphysical argument, as in Aquinas, Maimonides and Avicenna.

nodes.label: Deism
nodes.description: A rational creator made the world but does not intervene in it or reveal itself.

nodes.label: Reopened inquiry
nodes.description: After closure, the agent becomes willing to engage counterarguments and alternative hypotheses again.

nodes.label: Settled Judaism
nodes.description: Judaism embraced as a complete covenantal way of life under Torah, not as a step toward another tradition.

nodes.label: Settled Islam
nodes.description: Islam embraced as complete submission to one God through the Qur'an and the Prophet.

nodes.label: Fine-tuning argument
nodes.description: The narrow life-permitting range of physical constants is taken as evidence of design rather than chance.

nodes.label: Ontological argument
nodes.description: If a maximally great being is possible, it exists necessarily.

nodes.label: Argument from religious experience
nodes.description: Experiences of divine presence count as evidence, the way ordinary perception does, unless there is reason to doubt them.

nodes.label: Reformed epistemology
nodes.description: Belief in God can be properly basic, rational without resting on argument, like belief in other minds.

nodes.label: Argument from reason
nodes.description: If thought is fully produced by non-rational causes, it is hard to see how it can be trusted to track truth.

nodes.label: Evolutionary debunking
nodes.description: If moral and religious beliefs were selected for usefulness rather than truth, their seeming truth may need no further explanation.

nodes.label: Evidential problem of evil
nodes.description: The amount and distribution of suffering is much more expected without God than with one, even if the two are logically compatible.

edges.explanation: A person who notices they are inside a reality they did not make soon asks what that reality ultimately is. Metaphysics begins with that question.
Once a person takes their own place in reality seriously, the first question is how anything can be known at all. Epistemology comes before any claim about God or the world.
Some worldviews rest on claims about events in the past. Asking what actually happened turns the search toward history.
Everyone meets love and attachment before they meet arguments. That experience colors how every later question is weighed.
Most people feel the pull of obligation and the sting of guilt. That experience is part of what any worldview has to account for.
Every life meets suffering and death. That experience presses on every later question about God and meaning.
Before any worldview has earned priority, the honest starting place is not knowing. The person begins in radical uncertainty.
Asking what is ultimately real leads to why anything contingent exists at all. That opens the argument from contingency and sufficient reason.
Asking what is ultimately real opens the cosmological line of argument. If the universe is finite or caused, the kalam argument asks what caused it.
Asking what can be known turns attention to the knower. The fact of first-person experience becomes a piece of evidence in its own right.
Asking what happened leads to the most disputed figure in religious history. Jesus of Nazareth becomes a question for historians, not only for believers.
Love can feel like the deepest thing in reality rather than a by-product of it. That experience draws the person toward the love attractor.
The experience of obligation seems to present moral facts, not just feelings. Taken at face value, it supports objective value.
Suffering raises the question of how a wholly good and all-powerful God could allow it. That is the root of the problem of evil.
Suffering is not confined to humans; animals suffered for millions of years before us. That sharpens the problem, since free-will answers do not obviously reach it.
If everything contingent needs a reason for existing, the chain of reasons must end in something outside the contingent world. That makes a transcendent reality plausible.
If the cosmos began to exist or depends on a cause, its ground must lie outside it. That makes a transcendent reality plausible, though not yet a personal one.
If subjective experience resists reduction to physics, reality may contain more than the physical. That keeps a transcendent ground on the table.
If moral facts are real and binding, they need a ground that physical facts alone seem unable to supply. That points beyond contingent reality.
If persons have a unity and worth that matter alone does not seem to explain, reality may include more than matter. That lends modest support to transcendence.
Beauty that feels discovered rather than projected hints at a reality beyond the physical. The link is real but weak, so this is a gentle nudge.
If consciousness is basic rather than derived, the ground of reality may be mind-like. Reason and awareness start to look native to the universe, not accidental.
Objective moral duties look like the kind of thing a mind would issue, not an indifferent process. That shifts ultimate reality toward the mind-like.
If persons are irreducible and intrinsically valuable, the source of reality may itself be personal. Personhood becomes a clue about what is ultimate.
A transcendent ground could still be impersonal, so this step is tentative. It becomes personal theism only when the ground looks rational and purposive.
A transcendent reality need not be a person. It can be understood as an impersonal or nondual absolute, as in Vedanta and some mystical traditions.
A mind-like ground that supports reason, value and persons is most naturally read as personal. This is the strongest route into personal theism.
If moral facts are real and binding, they need a ground that can make demands on persons. A personal God is one candidate, though realists also defend moral facts as basic.

Once persons are seen to matter in themselves, the question is what could make that true. A personal God who knows and values each person is one natural answer, though humanists hold that dignity can be basic.
The argument from personhood first establishes that persons matter for their own sake. That dignity can later be grounded in different worldviews.
When no worldview has priority, naturalism stands out for its simplicity and its record in science. It becomes a strong contender.
If evil cannot logically coexist with a God who is all-powerful and wholly good, theism is simply false. Those who find the argument sound move directly toward naturalism.
Animal suffering over deep time seems to serve no purpose that involves animals themselves. Many find it among the strongest reasons to favor naturalism.
If a loving God wanted relationship, it is puzzling that so many sincere seekers find no sign of one. That silence is expected if there is no God, so it supports naturalism.
If revelation were real, one might expect more agreement about what was revealed. The sheer variety of faiths looks more like human invention, which supports naturalism.
Many accept that free-will defenses show God and evil are logically compatible, yet the defense leaves an uneasy residue. God stays plausible, but commitment gives way to uncertainty.
If a loving God stays hidden from sincere seekers, confidence in that God weakens. Theism survives as a possibility rather than a conviction.
Sincere, conflicting religious claims make it hard to trust any single revelation. Theism can survive this, but confident commitment usually does not.

edges.label: under unresolved evil/hiddenness
edges.explanation: Personal theism is held, but evil and hiddenness remain unresolved. The person stays open to God without being able to commit.

edges.label: if positive evidence accumulates
edges.explanation: If positive evidence keeps accumulating, the agnostic theist moves back toward confident personal theism. Uncertainty is a waiting room, not a dead end.

edges.label: if defeaters dominate
edges.explanation: If defeaters like evil and hiddenness dominate, theism stops being the best explanation. The person settles into naturalism while still unsure.

edges.label: evil objection presupposes morally significant suffering
edges.explanation: To call suffering evil is to assume that moral facts are real. The objection against God quietly relies on moral realism, feeding it back into the argument.
If moral claims are objective, they need an explanation. That strengthens the moral argument for a transcendent source of value.
If a personal God exists, it becomes reasonable to ask whether that God has spoken. Claims of revelation become evidence worth testing rather than dismissing.
Even uncertain theism leaves room for divine self-disclosure. Revelation opens as a possibility, though more tentatively than from confident theism.
Once revelation is possible, the question is which claims deserve attention. The traditions have to be compared on history, philosophy, ethics and experience.
Comparison leads to Judaism, the covenantal monotheism from which Christianity also grew. It can be embraced on its own terms or read as the first step toward the Christian claims.
Among the traditions compared, Christianity stands out for its claim that God acted in a specific historical person. That claim can be checked against history.
Comparison leads to Islam, which shares belief in one God who speaks through revelation. It is the closest alternative to test the Christian claims against.
Comparison leads to the Hindu traditions, with their range of views on the divine. Some are theistic and some describe an impersonal absolute.

edges.label: especially nondual / Vedantic trajectories
edges.explanation: Nondual and Vedantic Hindu thought identifies ultimate reality with Brahman beyond personal attributes. Following that path supports an impersonal absolute.

edges.label: tawhid / revelation
edges.explanation: Islam's insistence on one personal God who reveals himself strengthens personal theism itself. Looking elsewhere can end up reinforcing the shared foundation.

edges.label: historical and theological matrix
edges.explanation: Judaism supplies the setting that makes Jesus intelligible: his scriptures, expectations and categories. He is investigated as a first-century Jewish figure.
Christianity's claims all rest on Jesus of Nazareth. Testing them means turning to the historical figure at their center.
The historical Jesus leads directly to his execution, one of the best-attested facts about him. The crucifixion is common ground for believers and skeptics.
His followers proclaimed him risen soon after the crucifixion. That puts the resurrection claims at the center of the inquiry.
The early claim that the tomb was found empty is one of the data any explanation has to account for. It feeds directly into the resurrection question.
One live answer to the resurrection data is a natural one: visions, legend, memory or group dynamics. This branch keeps the explanation within nature.
The other live answer is that God actually raised Jesus. This branch takes the claim at face value as a historical event.

edges.label: if God exists, miracle prior rises
later Islamic interpretation creates tension with earlier crucifixion evidence
historical proximity favors earlier sources on Jesus' death

edges.explanation: If the resurrection happened, it becomes the gravitational center of the whole map. Nearly every later Christian belief depends on it.
Accepting the resurrection makes Christianity the best current explanation of the evidence. It is a leading hypothesis, not yet a settled commitment.
If the resurrection accounts are explained naturally, the main historical support for Christianity weakens. The balance tips toward naturalism.

edges.label: resurrection increases confidence in an acting personal God
edges.explanation: A real resurrection would be strong evidence of a God who acts in history. It raises confidence in personal theism after the fact.

edges.label: personal theism raises antecedent plausibility of miracle
edges.explanation: If a personal God exists, a miracle like the resurrection is not absurd in advance. Theism raises the starting plausibility of the claim.
If Christianity is the leading hypothesis, Jesus' own claims deserve new weight. His teaching becomes evidence rather than just history.
Taking Jesus' authority seriously raises the question of who he was. The inquiry turns from what he taught to what he is.
One answer is the incarnation: the Creator genuinely entered human life. Christology is interpreted through God becoming embodied.
Reflecting on Jesus' relation to the Father and the Spirit leads to the Trinity. Ultimate reality is reinterpreted as relational.
Christology also reframes the cross as an act of costly self-giving rather than a defeat. Evil is met from inside, not explained away.
If Jesus speaks with authority, earlier scripture is read through him. The texts are reinterpreted in light of the resurrection.
Reading scripture through Christ leads toward the community that preserved and practised it. Faith becomes communal and sacramental, not only intellectual.
Joining the apostolic community locates belief within historic creeds and sacraments. Christianity becomes a lived tradition, not only a hypothesis.
Once Christianity leads, the next step is to embrace it as a historic, lived faith. The hypothesis becomes a commitment.
If God truly became human, the historic creeds that affirm it gain support. The incarnation anchors commitment to historic Christianity.
The hope that death and suffering will be undone is central to historic Christianity. Embracing that hope draws the person into the full historic faith.

edges.label: relationality and love within ultimate reality
edges.explanation: If God's inner life is love between persons, love sits at the root of reality. The Trinity converges on the love attractor.
The intrinsic worth of persons fits naturally with a reality grounded in love. Dignity converges on the love attractor.

edges.label: existential coherence, not standalone proof
edges.explanation: A worldview that makes sense of love and dignity gains coherence, but coherence is not proof. Love lends Christianity support as the best overall fit.

edges.label: God enters suffering; does not show each evil serves a greater good
edges.explanation: The cross places God inside suffering rather than above it. That changes how suffering is faced, but it does not show that each evil serves a greater good.
The hope of restoration reframes suffering as something that will be healed, not simply ended. Evil is placed inside a larger story, though still unexplained.
The hope of restoration extends to all creation, not only to humans. It places animal suffering inside a story of healing, though it does not explain why that suffering was allowed.
If God became human, God's presence was once concrete and visible. That softens divine hiddenness a little, but only a little.
Harm from a religious community can make further inquiry feel unsafe. The person may stop engaging with the question at all.

edges.label: one possible settling state
edges.explanation: When inquiry closes, the default often becomes naturalism. It is one possible settling point, reached by disengagement rather than argument.
Naturalism leaves the question of how to live. Secular humanism keeps human dignity and ethics without appealing to God.
Without a purpose built into the cosmos, meaning has to be made rather than found. Humanism settles into constructed meaning.
Secular humanism has to say where morality comes from without God. It turns to naturalistic accounts that ground, reconstruct or deflate moral claims.

If a good God and evil cannot both exist, theism is refuted outright and naturalism is left as the default. The pull is only as strong as the incompatibility premise, which free-will defenses contest.
If God is hidden from sincere seekers, the simplest explanation may be that there is no God to find. Hiddenness feeds naturalistic simplicity.
Millions of years of animal pain before any human existed fit a blind natural process better than a good design. That feeds the naturalistic-simplicity attractor.
Once simplicity dominates, naturalism becomes the preferred worldview. The attractor settles the person in agnostic naturalism.

edges.label: human love/value can be retained without theism

edges.explanation: Persons can be treated as ends without grounding their worth in God. Dignity supports secular humanism as well as theism.
Historic Christian commitment is held honestly, with evil, hiddenness and pluralism still unresolved. Faith settles, but the questions stay open.
The problem of evil remains a live pressure inside Christian commitment. Believers carry it rather than solve it.
The problem of evil does not disappear on the Christian path. It becomes a residual tension that believers must keep working through.
The argument from consciousness does not disappear on the naturalist path. It becomes a residual tension that naturalism must still explain.
Consciousness remains a live pressure on naturalism. Naturalists carry it as an open problem rather than a solved one.
If moral facts are real, persons seem to have intrinsic worth. Naturalism must explain that worth, which leaves a residual tension.

edges.label: if the case against God seems decisive
edges.explanation: An agnostic naturalist who judges the case for God outweighed, not just unproven, moves from suspending judgment to denial. Atheism is a positive claim, so it carries its own burden of argument.

edges.label: if confidence in denial softens
edges.explanation: An atheist who grants that the arguments against God fall short of proof steps back to suspending judgment. Naturalism stays favored, but the verdict becomes open.
If the scale of suffering is much more likely without God than with one, it counts as evidence that there is no God. That supports atheism, not just doubt.
If contingent things need a sufficient reason, the chain ends in something that exists necessarily. Classical theism identifies that necessary being with God as the ground of being.
Once a transcendent reality is plausible, one natural way to understand it is as being itself, simple and unconditioned. That is the God of classical theism.

edges.label: if the ground of being is also personal
edges.explanation: Classical theists already ascribe intellect and will to the ground of being, analogically. Emphasizing a God who knows, loves and acts in history brings the view into personal theism.
Asking what a personal God must be to be truly ultimate leads to simplicity, necessity and self-existence. Personal theism deepens into the classical account of God as being itself.

edges.label: if the metaphysical arguments feel inconclusive
edges.explanation: If the arguments for a necessary ground seem valid but their premises uncertain, confidence gives way. God remains plausible, but commitment becomes tentative.

edges.label: if the metaphysical arguments firm up
edges.explanation: If the contingency or ontological argument comes to seem sound, uncertain theism can settle on God as the necessary ground of being. The route runs through metaphysics rather than history or experience.
A mind-like ground can be accepted without any belief that it intervenes or reveals itself. Deism holds that the world has a rational source that leaves it to run.

edges.label: if no revelation seems credible
edges.explanation: If the ground of being is accepted but claims of revelation and miracle seem unconvincing, God becomes the author of the world rather than an actor in it. That is deism.
Uncertain theism can resolve by keeping a creator while dropping a God who acts in history. Deism asks less of the evidence than personal theism does.
If God seems silent, a creator who does not intervene explains that silence well. Hiddenness is a problem for a loving, present God but not for a distant one.

edges.label: if revelation or experience lands
edges.explanation: If a credible revelation or a personal religious experience lands, the distant creator starts to look like one who speaks and acts. Deism opens into personal theism.
A creator who never acts leaves no trace the world cannot explain on its own. On grounds of simplicity, some deists drop the creator and settle into naturalism.
Judaism can be embraced as a complete way of life under the covenant, with Torah and the God of Israel. It is a settled position in its own right, not only a step toward Christianity.
Jewish commitment still meets the Christian claim that a Jewish teacher rose from the dead. Weighing that claim puts the historical question of the resurrection in view.

edges.label: candidate for global explanatory fit
edges.explanation: Settled Judaism offers its own account of God, law, history and suffering. It competes with the other settled positions for the best overall fit.
Islam can be embraced as complete submission to one God through the Qur'an and the Prophet. It is a settled position of strict monotheism, not a waystation.

The Qur'an (4:157) is traditionally read as denying that Jesus was crucified, while most historians treat the crucifixion as near certain. A settled Muslim weighs that reading against the historical record, and some interpreters read the verse more narrowly.

edges.label: candidate for global explanatory fit
edges.explanation: Settled Islam offers its own account of God, revelation, law and judgment. It competes with the other settled positions for the best overall fit.

Some Buddhist traditions point to an unconditioned reality such as nirvana or Buddha-nature, without a creator or permanent self. That reframes the ultimate as impersonal, though Madhyamaka denies any absolute ground.

edges.label: if defeaters weaken or tensions accumulate
edges.explanation: If the case from evil and hiddenness loses force, or the tensions around consciousness and value keep building, naturalism no longer looks clearly best. The person reopens theism while still unsure.
If consciousness keeps resisting physical explanation, some conclude mind is fundamental, as panpsychism, idealism or a cosmic mind. Only the last makes a mind-like ground of reality a live option.

If brute existence and the universe's intelligibility still lack explanation, a rational ground becomes attractive. Naturalists reply that explanation must stop at some brute fact, and theism has one too.
If reasons and the norms of good thinking will not reduce to physical facts, then some normative facts are real. That reopens moral realism.
If persons seem to have a worth that no evolutionary story fully explains, the naturalist is led to treat that worth as intrinsic. Intrinsic dignity then asks for a ground.

edges.label: what grounds meaning?
edges.explanation: Constructed meaning works in practice, but some lives and choices seem to matter whatever anyone decides. Pressing that question leads toward the intrinsic worth of persons.

edges.label: what grounds meaning?
edges.explanation: Much of the meaning people build centers on love, which often feels received rather than invented. That points meaning toward love as something found in reality, not only made.
Naturalistic moral realists hold that moral facts are real. Taking that realism seriously raises the broader question of objective value and what grounds it.
If moral facts are identified with natural facts, it remains unclear how natural facts can bind or give reasons. That keeps the tension around normativity alive.
If naturalism stays highly competitive after honest inquiry, many settle there while keeping the deepest questions open. That is agnostic naturalism.
Some judge that naturalism is not only competitive but clearly the better explanation. They conclude that there is no God.

edges.label: if the absolute seems to know and love
edges.explanation: If ultimate reality seems to include awareness, will and love, the impersonal picture looks incomplete. The absolute starts to look personal.

An impersonal absolute and the classical God share much: both are simple, necessary and beyond ordinary categories. Treating that absolute as the source of the world moves the view toward classical theism.
Uncertain theism can resolve by keeping a transcendent reality while letting go of a personal God. Vedantic and some mystical traditions describe the absolute that way.

edges.label: after the harm is addressed
edges.explanation: Closure is often a defense against real harm. When that harm is named and addressed, the person can afford to engage the questions again.
Forgiving, or being forgiven, can lower the defenses that closure put up. Reconciliation makes it safe to reopen questions that had been shut.
Reopened inquiry often starts from not knowing. The person returns to open uncertainty rather than straight to a new position.
Some who reopen the questions find that God is again a live possibility. They take up theism tentatively, without the old certainties.
Apparent contradictions and hard passages make it harder to read scripture as one unified witness to Christ. They press against the Christian rereading of scripture.
Many believers keep their commitment while living with unresolved textual problems. Those problems become part of what Christian commitment carries.
Asking what is ultimately real includes asking why the physical constants permit life at all. That opens the fine-tuning argument.

If life-permitting constants are far more likely given a designing mind than given chance, fine-tuning is evidence for a mind-like ground. Multiverse and observer-selection replies contest how much it shows.
If the laws and constants need an explanation beyond themselves, that explanation lies outside the physical universe. Transcendence becomes plausible.
Asking what is ultimately real leads to whether a greatest possible being could fail to exist. That is the question of the ontological argument.
If a maximally great being is even possible, modal versions of the argument conclude that it exists necessarily. Many find the possibility premise the weak point, so the pull is modest.
Experiences of divine presence are reported across cultures and eras. Treating them as evidence turns experience into an argument.
Asking what can be known includes whether experience can be trusted when it seems to show God. By the principle of credulity, things are presumed to be as they appear unless there is reason to doubt.
If religious experiences are trusted unless defeated, as ordinary perception is, their frequency supports a transcendent reality. Critics point to their diversity and to natural explanations.
Many religious experiences feel like meeting someone, not something. If they are veridical, ultimate reality is personal.
Asking what can be known includes which beliefs need argument at all. Some beliefs, like belief in other minds, seem rational without proof.
Reformed epistemology holds that belief in God can be properly basic, like trust in memory or other minds. A believer can then be rational without winning every argument.
If belief in God does not rest on winning debates, endless argument loses its power to wear faith down. That undercuts argument fatigue.
Asking what can be known includes whether our reasoning can be trusted. That opens the argument from reason.
If beliefs are fully caused by non-rational processes, it is hard to see how they are held for good reasons. That sharpens the tension around normativity within naturalism.
If naturalism undercuts trust in the reasoning used to argue for it, its simplicity comes at a cost. Naturalists reply that natural selection favors reliable cognition.
If our faculties were shaped for survival, it is fair to ask whether they track truth about morality and religion. That is the evolutionary debunking argument.
If moral intuitions were selected for usefulness, their seeming truth may be explained without moral facts. Realists reply that the same argument would undercut many other beliefs.
If a tendency to detect agents and purposes was adaptive, religious experience may be explained without God. Believers answer that explaining how a belief arises does not show it false.

If evolution explains our moral sense without moral facts, morality looks like an adaptation rather than a discovery. That mainly supports anti-realist or constructivist naturalism, since the same dilemma presses naturalist realists.
Suffering on the scale and in the forms we see raises a question of probability. It can count as evidence against God even if God and evil are logically compatible.
Suffering that appears to serve no greater good is more expected if there is no God. Many who find that weighty but not decisive lean naturalist while staying unsure.

If God would prevent pointless suffering, and some suffering seems pointless, a good and powerful God becomes less probable. Skeptical theists reply that we are poorly placed to judge which evils are pointless.

edges.label: if the tensions outweigh the case
edges.explanation: If evil, hiddenness and textual problems come to outweigh the positive case, commitment loosens. The person steps back to an uncertain theism.

edges.label: candidate for global explanatory fit
edges.explanation: Atheism offers a complete account of the world without God. It competes with the other settled positions for the best overall fit.
Believing in a God who is all-powerful and wholly good is what makes suffering a problem at all. The more seriously someone holds personal theism, the sharper the evidential problem becomes.
If moral facts are real, among the most secure of them is that persons must not be used as mere things. Moral realism makes the intrinsic dignity of persons hard to deny.
Jewish tradition holds that the messianic age has not arrived and that God is not incarnate. A Christian has to answer why Israel's own interpreters did not see Jesus as the promised messiah.
Islam presents itself as restoring a strict monotheism that the doctrine of the Trinity obscured. A Christian has to show that the Trinity is monotheism rather than a departure from it.

edges.label: candidate for global explanatory fit
edges.explanation: Classical theism explains why anything exists at all by grounding it in a necessary being. It competes with the other settled positions for the best overall fit.

edges.label: candidate for global explanatory fit
edges.explanation: Deism explains the order of the world with a creator while asking nothing of miracle or revelation. It competes with the other settled positions for the best overall fit.
Suffering that seems pointless lowers confidence in God without settling the question. Many stay open to God but can no longer commit.

cycles.label: Theism ↔ Resurrection Bayesian loop
cycles.description: Theism raises the prior plausibility of resurrection; resurrection, if judged likely, then increases confidence in personal theism.

cycles.label: Problem of evil ↔ Moral realism loop
cycles.description: Evil pressures against theism, while the moral force of the objection itself can generate questions about objective value and its metaphysical grounding.

cycles.label: Resurrection → Christ → Scripture → worldview reinterpretation
cycles.description: Historical confidence in resurrection upgrades Jesus' authority; Christ then changes the interpretation of scripture, metaphysics, suffering, and revelation.

cycles.label: Naturalist explanatory reinforcement
cycles.description: Suffering and hiddenness favor naturalism; naturalism then lowers miracle priors and can further reduce the probability assigned to resurrection.

cycles.label: Love ↔ Christian ontology loop
cycles.description: Human love creates existential/metaphysical pressure; Christian doctrines interpret love as reflecting ultimate reality, which can increase perceived worldview coherence.

cycles.label: Deconstruction → closure reinforcement
cycles.description: Institutional failure or trauma can weaken trust, reduce willingness to revisit evidence, and stabilize a secular or agnostic state independently of purely analytic argument.

tours.label: Ascent 1: from first questions to personal theism
tours.description: The cosmological route: a question about what is ultimately real branches to the kalam argument, which makes transcendence plausible, which opens onto personal theism. Every theistic argument in the map funnels through this same gateway.

tours.label: Ascent 2: from personal theism to the resurrection question
tours.description: Personal theism opens the possibility of revelation, which leads into comparative religion and then, through Judaism and the historical Jesus, to the question of what explains the resurrection data.

tours.label: Ascent 3: from the resurrection bottleneck to settled commitment
tours.description: If the resurrection is judged actual, it converges on the resurrection attractor and makes Christianity the leading hypothesis. Christ, scripture and church follow, and the path settles in Christian commitment that still carries unresolved tensions.

tours.label: Stalled theism: when theism does not open to revelation
tours.description: From consciousness, the path reaches personal theism, then turns toward tentative theism instead of revelation, and from there drifts to agnostic naturalism.

tours.label: Suffering to constructed meaning
tours.description: The shortest collapse in the map: the logical problem of evil leads directly to agnostic naturalism, then secular humanism, and ends at meaning constructed rather than discovered. From there the only ways on are questions about what grounds meaning.

tours.label: Personhood fork A: toward love
tours.description: Starting from the argument from personhood, intrinsic dignity converges on the love attractor, which supports Christianity as the leading hypothesis.

tours.label: Personhood fork B: toward humanism
tours.description: The same first step as fork A, but intrinsic dignity supports secular humanism instead, which interprets meaning as constructed rather than discovered.

tours.label: What Christian commitment still carries
tours.description: The problem of evil does not disappear on the Christian path. It becomes a residual tension that keeps pressure on Christian commitment.

tours.label: What naturalism still carries
tours.description: The argument from consciousness does not disappear on the naturalist path. It becomes a residual tension that keeps pressure on agnostic naturalism.

tours.label: From a person inside reality to committed faith, with tensions
tours.description: The longest route in the map from Human person inside reality to Christian commitment with unresolved tensions that never revisits a concept: 20 steps. Along the way it passes Personal theism, Revelation becomes a live possibility, Comparative religious investigation, What best explains the resurrection data?, Attractor: Resurrection, and Christianity leading hypothesis. Long routes double back through the core, the way a lived journey does.

tours.label: Convinced, unsettled by suffering, tests other faiths, returns
tours.description: Someone already persuaded that Christianity is the leading hypothesis follows it into the meaning of the cross, where the problem of evil resurfaces. Unsettled, they step back to uncertain theism, reopen the question of revelation and test Islam. That strengthens their belief in one personal God, which raises the plausibility of the resurrection again. They return to Christianity and go further than before, into historic commitment that still carries its tensions.

tours.label: Convinced, unsettled by hiddenness, re-examines the history, returns
tours.description: Someone persuaded of Christianity reflects on the incarnation, and the hiddenness of God becomes a real problem. They fall back to uncertain theism, and only as positive evidence accumulates do they return to personal theism. They reopen revelation, compare the traditions, and re-examine the history from Jesus through the crucifixion to the resurrection question. The resurrection holds, so they come back to Christianity and settle into historic commitment, tensions included.

tours.label: Convinced, unsettled by suffering, lives as a humanist, returns
tours.description: Someone who believes in a personal God finds that belief is what makes suffering so hard to explain. The evidential problem moves them to agnostic naturalism, and they live as a secular humanist who builds their own meaning. In time the question of why persons matter at all leads them to intrinsic dignity, and from there back to a personal God. This time they test the claims of revelation and settle in Judaism, a tradition that makes room for arguing with God about suffering, as Job does.

profiles.label: Default
profiles.description: The global weights, with every argument felt at the strength the map gives it.

profiles.label: Evidentialist
profiles.description: Moved by public evidence and historical argument, and wary of private experience and purely a priori proofs.

profiles.label: Existential
profiles.description: Moved by lived experience of love, suffering, beauty and meaning more than by formal argument or historical reconstruction.

profiles.label: Moral realist
profiles.description: Treats moral knowledge as among the most secure things we know, so moral arguments carry weight and debunking arguments do not.

profiles.label: Empiricist
profiles.description: Trusts science and observation, and discounts a priori metaphysics and arguments that outrun experience.

profiles.label: Rationalist
profiles.description: Moved by a priori and metaphysical argument, and less by historical reconstruction.

attractors.role: Christian falsification and recursive confirmation node
Convergence node for personhood, value, self-giving, cross, and Trinity
Attractor generated by suffering, hiddenness, scientific continuity, and low miracle priors
Global inference-to-best-explanation attractor across all evidence families

recommended_runtime_behavior: Allow node weights or priors to be adjusted per agent.
Allow edge weights to vary by agent history, trust, background, and current worldview.
Compute signed incoming pressure separately from transition probability.
Do not assume a DAG; feedback loops are intentional.
Consider attractor strength, hysteresis, and epistemic closure as separate from raw evidential weight.
Permit historical, analytic, experiential, and social edges to be toggled independently.
Track path history because the same node may be interpreted differently depending on traversal order.

stages.name: Pre-theoretical experience
stages.description: Raw human experience and initial worldview uncertainty.

stages.name: Foundational inquiry
stages.description: Epistemology, metaphysics, logic, consciousness, morality, contingency, and intelligibility.

stages.name: Major worldview formation
stages.description: Naturalism, personal theism, impersonal/transpersonal ultimate reality, and agnostic intermediates.

stages.name: Revelation possibility
stages.description: Whether a personal transcendent reality could disclose itself.

stages.name: Comparative religion
stages.description: Competing traditions, revelation claims, and religious explanatory systems.

stages.name: Historical investigation
stages.description: Historical Jesus, crucifixion, early Christian claims, and competing explanations.

stages.name: Resurrection bottleneck
stages.description: The resurrection question as Christianity's principal falsification and convergence gateway.

stages.name: Christian interpretive expansion
stages.description: Christology, incarnation, cross, Trinity, scripture, restoration, and recursive reinterpretation.

stages.name: Ecclesial differentiation
stages.description: Church, sacrament, apostolic continuity, and historic Christian commitment.

unlockSemantics.allOf: Every listed prerequisite must be explored or accepted.
unlockSemantics.anyOf: At least one listed prerequisite must be explored or accepted.
unlockSemantics.note: Prerequisites indicate epistemic availability, not deductive entailment.

layoutIntent.globalNodes: Render outside normal stage columns as persistent environmental modifiers.
layoutIntent.backwardEdges: Render as large curved arcs above or below the main progression lanes.
layoutIntent.feedbackEdges: Render distinctly from ordinary backward transitions.
layoutIntent.defeaterEdges: Visually distinguish signed negative pressure from ordinary branching.

stateEffects.description: If personal theism is accepted, miracle claims no longer carry the same naturalistic prior penalty.
A judged-likely resurrection recursively increases confidence in an acting personal God.
Resurrection functions as a credibility multiplier for Jesus' claims.
The cross reframes divine relation to suffering but does not eliminate the evidential problem.
Cosmic restoration changes the Christian interpretation of suffering without fully resolving why it was permitted.
Naturalism further lowers the antecedent plausibility of a miracle explanation.
Epistemic closure reduces responsiveness to reopening arguments regardless of nominal graph weight.
